\section{Introduction}
Games such as Werewolf and Mafia combine hidden roles, public actions, deception, and repeated elimination. The common instruction to vote for the player most likely to be an adversary conflates two statements: that the player is most likely to hold the hidden role, and that selecting that player maximizes eventual victory. The first is classification; the second is sequential control. Posterior probability describes belief, while utility describes consequences.

We establish the finite mathematics that distinguishes these claims. The immediate hit utility makes expected correctness exactly equal to the selected posterior. A continuation model with identity-independent values for hits and misses remains affine in that posterior and therefore preserves its ordering. Once consequences depend on identity, however, posterior and utility rankings can diverge.

The analysis also introduces a centered coordinate in which binary role probabilities behave like mean spins. The results are foundational rather than a calculation of a particular full-game win rate: such a calculation additionally requires transition rules, observation channels, and policies for both teams.

\section{Finite Bayesian model}
Let $I$ be a finite, nonempty set of suspects. For each $i\in I$, let $\pi_i$ be a prior weight and $L_i$ the likelihood of the observed evidence under hypothesis $i$. Define
\[
w_i=\pi_iL_i,\qquad Z=\sum_{j\in I}w_j.
\]
When $Z\neq0$, define the posterior coordinate by $p_i=w_i/Z$. Standard probabilistic use assumes nonnegative priors and likelihoods and hence $Z>0$ whenever some hypothesis has positive weight.

\begin{theorem}[Finite posterior normalization]
If $Z\neq0$, then $\sum_{i\in I}p_i=1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Factoring the common denominator gives
\[
\sum_i p_i=\frac{\sum_iw_i}{Z}=\frac ZZ=1.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Positive normalization preserves order]
If $Z>0$, then for all $i,j\in I$,
\[
p_i\le p_j\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w_i\le w_j.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Both posterior coordinates have the same positive denominator. Multiplication by $Z$ preserves the inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
A suspect $a\in I$ is \emph{maximum-a-posteriori}, or MAP, if $p_i\le p_a$ for every $i\in I$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Existence of a MAP action]
Every real-valued posterior score on a finite nonempty suspect set has a MAP action.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The finite nonempty set $\{p_i:i\in I\}$ has a maximum; any index attaining it is MAP.
\end{proof}

\section{Immediate correctness}
For action $a$ and true hidden identity $w$, define
\[
u_{\rm hit}(a,w)=\begin{cases}1,&a=w,\\0,&a\neq w.\end{cases}
\]
For any utility $u:I\times I\to\mathbb R$, define posterior expected utility by
\[
U_p(a;u)=\sum_{w\in I}p_wu(a,w).
\]

\begin{lemma}[Expected correctness identity]
For every $a\in I$, $U_p(a;u_{\rm hit})=p_a$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every term in the expectation vanishes except $w=a$, leaving $p_a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Local MAP Optimality]
If $a$ is MAP, then for every $b\in I$,
\[
U_p(b;u_{\rm hit})\le U_p(a;u_{\rm hit}).
\]
Thus a MAP elimination maximizes the probability that the present elimination is correct.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The expected utilities are $p_b$ and $p_a$, respectively, and the MAP property gives $p_b\le p_a$.
\end{proof}

This conclusion is independent of the source of the evidence. Voting histories, survival events, speech, and other observations may all enter the likelihood. The theorem begins after those data have been summarized by a posterior. It is local because its objective is the present hit indicator, not an entire trajectory.

\section{Identity-symmetric continuation}
Let $G$ be continuation value after a correct elimination and $B$ value after an incorrect elimination. Define
\[
u_{G,B}(a,w)=\begin{cases}G,&a=w,\\B,&a\neq w.\end{cases}
\]
Identity symmetry means that value depends on hit versus miss but not on the selected name.

\begin{theorem}[Affine Continuation Formula]
If $\sum_i p_i=1$, then
\[
U_p(a;u_{G,B})=B+(G-B)p_a.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Separate state $w=a$ from the remaining states:
\[
U_p(a;u_{G,B})=p_aG+\sum_{w\ne a}p_wB
=p_aG+(1-p_a)B.
\]
Rearranging yields the result.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetric Continuation Optimality]
Assume $\sum_i p_i=1$ and $B\le G$. If $a$ is MAP, then for every $b\in I$,
\[
U_p(b;u_{G,B})\le U_p(a;u_{G,B}).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The affine formula gives
\[
U_p(a;u_{G,B})-U_p(b;u_{G,B})=(G-B)(p_a-p_b).
\]
Both factors are nonnegative.
\end{proof}

If $G=B$, all actions tie; if $G<B$, the order reverses. In a sequential game, $G$ and $B$ may summarize all later play. The theorem applies only if that value-to-go is exchangeable over surviving identities after conditioning on hit or miss. Different powers, social influence, information revelation, coalition effects, or future observation channels can violate this condition.

\section{Approximation regret}
\begin{theorem}[Posterior Approximation Regret Bound]
Assume $\sum_i p_i=1$ and $B\le G$. If actions $a,b\in I$ satisfy $p_a\le p_b+\varepsilon$, then
\[
U_p(a;u_{G,B})-U_p(b;u_{G,B})\le (G-B)\varepsilon.
\]
In particular, choosing an action within $\varepsilon$ of the maximal posterior loses at most $(G-B)\varepsilon$ continuation value.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The value difference is $(G-B)(p_a-p_b)$. The hypothesis bounds the second factor by $\varepsilon$, and $G-B$ is nonnegative.
\end{proof}

The bound is sharp when $p_a-p_b=\varepsilon$. It separates inferential error $\varepsilon$ from strategic sensitivity $G-B$.

\section{Failure without identity symmetry}
\begin{theorem}[Two-suspect counterexample]
A unique MAP action can have strictly smaller expected continuation value than another action when correct-hit rewards depend on identity.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Take two suspects with
\[
p_0=\frac35,\qquad p_1=\frac25.
\]
A correct elimination of suspect $0$ has value $1/10$, a correct elimination of suspect $1$ has value $1$, and every miss has value $0$. Suspect $0$ is MAP, but
\[
U_p(0)=\frac35\frac1{10}=\frac3{50}=0.06
<\frac25=\frac25\cdot1=U_p(1).
\]
Thus the lower-posterior action is better.
\end{proof}

This is not a failure of Bayesian reasoning. Expected-utility maximization correctly selects suspect $1$. It is a failure of replacing utility with probability when action consequences are heterogeneous. If action-specific hit rewards are $R_i$ and misses are worth zero, actions are ranked by $p_iR_i$, not generally by $p_i$.

\section{Centered posteriors and spin symmetry}
\begin{definition}
The centered posterior score is $s(p)=2p-1$.
\end{definition}
For $p\in[0,1]$, this maps probability to $[-1,1]$, with $p=1/2$ mapped to zero.

\begin{theorem}[Order preservation]
For all real $p,q$,
\[
s(p)\le s(q)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\le q.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The map $p\mapsto2p-1$ is strictly increasing.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Role complementation is spin flip]
For every real $p$,
\[
s(1-p)=-s(p).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Expanding gives $2(1-p)-1=1-2p=-(2p-1)$.
\end{proof}

Consider sites $(x,y)$ with $0\le x\le m$ and $0\le y\le n$. There are $(m+1)(n+1)$ sites. Define magnetization of a field $\sigma$ by
\[
M(\sigma)=\sum_{x=0}^{m}\sum_{y=0}^{n}\sigma(x,y).
\]

\begin{theorem}[Constant Posterior Magnetization]
If $\sigma(x,y)=s(p)$ at every site, then
\[
M(\sigma)=(m+1)(n+1)s(p).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The sum contains $(m+1)(n+1)$ identical terms.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Complementation reverses magnetization]
Complementing every posterior from $p$ to $1-p$ changes $M$ to $-M$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Every site score changes sign, and summation is linear.
\end{proof}

The correspondence is exact for centered one-site marginals and constant fields. A complete interacting-spin representation of correlated role assignments would additionally require a joint likelihood and a fixed-role-count constraint.

\section{Algorithms and numerical examples}
MAP selection computes $w_i=\pi_iL_i$, sums $Z$, normalizes if calibrated probabilities are required, and returns an index maximizing $w_i$. It uses $O(N)$ time for $N$ suspects. Storage is $O(N)$ when all posteriors are retained and $O(1)$ auxiliary space when only an argmax is needed. For long evidence sequences, log-weights and log-sum-exp avoid numerical underflow.

Symmetric continuation values are computed as $V_i=B+(G-B)p_i$ in $O(N)$ time. When $B\le G$, their ordering is already known to match posterior ordering. With identity-dependent hit rewards $R_i$ and zero miss values, comparing $p_iR_i$ with $p_i$ provides an $O(N)$ diagnostic for disagreement between posterior and utility rankings.

For example, let
\[
\pi=(0.4,0.35,0.25),\qquad L=(0.2,0.8,0.5).
\]
Then $w=(0.08,0.28,0.125)$, $Z=0.485$, and
\[
p\approx(0.16495,0.57732,0.25773).
\]
The second suspect is MAP. With $G=0.9$ and $B=0.2$,
\[
V=0.2+0.7p\approx(0.31546,0.60412,0.38041),
\]
so the same suspect is optimal.

At $p=0.7$, the centered score is $0.4$. A $4$-by-$5$ array has magnetization $20(0.4)=8$. Complementation gives $p=0.3$, score $-0.4$, and magnetization $-8$.

\section{Applications and limitations}
The distinction applies to medical testing, cybersecurity, fraud review, and active learning. Selecting the most likely positive case maximizes immediate hits under zero-one reward. Urgency, criticality, transaction size, information gain, and downstream effects introduce identity-dependent utilities and can rationally favor a lower-posterior action.

No particular Werewolf win probability follows from these one-step results. A full model must specify role revelation, ties, day--night order, night targeting, evidence generation, updating, sampling without replacement, and terminal conditions. Nor does MAP optimality establish a scaling law such as
\[
C\left(1-\frac{k}{n-k}\right)^2.
\]
The constant and functional form depend on the information channel and transition process.

With exactly $k$ wolves among $n$ players, a complete posterior is a distribution over $k$-element subsets. Selecting the largest marginal still maximizes the chance that the selected player is a wolf, but future value can depend on the joint posterior.

\section{Future directions}
Promising extensions include an adaptive-submodularity criterion for greedy posterior voting; a signal-to-noise threshold for value of information; parity-sensitive asymptotics in information-free games; constrained spin-system representations of correlated voting histories; and horizon-sensitive regret bounds for approximate posterior policies. Each direction extends a boundary isolated here: modular one-step utility, concentration rather than ranking, paired day--night losses, one-site spin symmetry, or one-step approximation regret.

\section{Conclusion}
MAP voting always maximizes immediate correctness in a finite posterior model. It also maximizes continuation value when the future distinguishes only hit from miss, treats identities exchangeably, and values a hit at least as highly. In that setting continuation value is affine in the selected posterior and approximation regret is bounded sharply by $(G-B)\varepsilon$.

Identity-dependent consequences invalidate an unrestricted global claim. The general prescription is to maximize expected utility; MAP is the important special case produced by zero-one or identity-symmetric rewards. Centered posterior scores further reveal an exact spin-flip symmetry, linking posterior ranking, role complementation, and magnetization in a common representation.

concept.title: Proofs as DAGs: The Directed Acyclic Graph Structure of Mathematics
concept.concept_description: Every mathematical proof is a directed acyclic graph (DAG): nodes are statements, edges are implications, and the acyclicity comes from the fact that you can't prove A from B and B from A without a circular argument (which is not a valid proof). import Bridges.PigeonholeInjectionBridge

/-!
# Ranked Dependency Networks: Width, Depth, and Robustness

A dependency network is represented by a relation `R`, oriented from a premise to a
statement using that premise.  Acyclicity means that the transitive closure has no
self-loop.  This development separates three structural facts from empirical claims
about large mathematical corpora.

First, every finite acyclic network has a canonical topological rank: the number of
strict ancestors.  Second, combining this rank with the pigeonhole principle gives a
width–depth theorem: if there are more statements than available rank levels, two
statements on one level are incomparable.  Third, a family of totally ordered dependency
networks remains weakly connected after deletion of any one nonterminal vertex.  Thus
acyclicity alone neither implies a power law nor universal hub-removal fragility.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): finite acyclicity should force a topological hierarchy, but
neither a heavy-tailed degree law nor articulation hubs.  A depth bound should instead
force width by a pigeonhole argument.

Experiment (Experimenter): rank each node by the cardinality of its transitive
predecessor set; test deletion on strict total-order networks, where every surviving
pair remains joined by a direct edge in one orientation.

Analysis (Analyst): reachability strictly enlarges predecessor sets, producing the
ranking.  Bounded ranks then create an incomparable pair whenever the vertex count
exceeds the number of levels.  Total-order networks provide robust acyclic examples,
contradicting any graph-theoretic derivation of fragility from acyclicity alone.

Critique (Critic): the results do not estimate a degree-distribution exponent and do
not identify historical theorems as hubs; those are empirical questions requiring a
specified corpus and dependency extraction policy.  Connectivity is explicitly weak
connectivity of the surviving directed network, avoiding an ambiguous use of
"disconnects".  Nonemptiness and cardinality hypotheses prevent vacuity.

Synthesis (Principal Investigator): finite proof structure yields a rigorous
order-theoretic width–depth law, while a concrete robust family establishes the boundary
between structural theorem and corpus-dependent hypothesis.
-- !-- end Lab Notes -- !--
-/

open scoped Classical

namespace ProofDAGStructure

variable {V : Type*}

/-- A direct dependency relation is acyclic when its nonempty transitive closure is
irreflexive. -/
def Acyclic (R : V → V → Prop) : Prop := ∀ v, ¬ Relation.TransGen R v v

/-- The strict ancestors of a node in a finite dependency network. -/
noncomputable def ancestors [Fintype V] (R : V → V → Prop) (v : V) : Finset V :=
  Finset.univ.filter (fun u => Relation.TransGen R u v)

/-
Reachability carries every ancestor of the source to an ancestor of the target.
-/
lemma ancestors_mono [Fintype V] {R : V → V → Prop} {a b : V}
    (hab : Relation.TransGen R a b) : ancestors R a ⊆ ancestors R b := by
  intro v hv
  simp [ancestors] at hv;
  exact Finset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨ Finset.mem_univ _, hv.trans hab ⟩

/-
Along a dependency chain, the ancestor set grows strictly.
-/
lemma ancestors_ssubset [Fintype V] {R : V → V → Prop} (hR : Acyclic R)
    {a b : V} (hab : Relation.TransGen R a b) : ancestors R a ⊂ ancestors R b := by
  convert Finset.ssubset_iff_subset_ne.2 ⟨ ancestors_mono hab, ?_ ⟩;
  simp_all +decide [ Finset.ext_iff, ancestors ];
  exact ⟨ a, by have := hR a; tauto ⟩

/-
Every finite acyclic dependency network has a canonical topological numbering,
given by the number of strict ancestors.
-/
theorem canonical_topological_rank [Fintype V] {R : V → V → Prop} (hR : Acyclic R) :
    ∀ {a b : V}, Relation.TransGen R a b →
      (ancestors R a).card < (ancestors R b).card := by
  intro a b hab;
  apply Finset.card_lt_card; exact ancestors_ssubset hR hab;

/-
A bounded topological ranking with fewer levels than vertices forces two distinct,
mutually incomparable statements on the same level.  This is a width–depth tradeoff
obtained by bridging acyclic order structure with the finite pigeonhole principle.
-/
theorem incomparable_pair_of_rank_bound [Fintype V] {R : V → V → Prop}
    (levels : ℕ) (rank : V → Fin levels)
    (hrank : ∀ {a b : V}, Relation.TransGen R a b → rank a < rank b)
    (hcard : levels < Fintype.card V) :
    ∃ a b : V, a ≠ b ∧ ¬ Relation.TransGen R a b ∧ ¬ Relation.TransGen R b a := by
  obtain ⟨a, b, hab, heq⟩ :=
    PigeonholeInjectionBridge.pigeonhole rank (by simpa using hcard)
  exact ⟨a, b, hab, fun h => heq.not_lt (hrank h),
    fun h => heq.not_gt (hrank h)⟩

/-- Weak reachability while avoiding a deleted vertex: each step may follow a dependency
edge in either direction, and every visited endpoint must survive. -/
inductive AvoidingWalk (R : V → V → Prop) (deleted : V) : V → V → Prop
  | refl {a} (ha : a ≠ deleted) : AvoidingWalk R deleted a a
  | step {a b c} (ha : a ≠ deleted) (hab : R a b ∨ R b a)
      (hbc : AvoidingWalk R deleted b c) : AvoidingWalk R deleted a c

/-- The strict total-order dependency network on `Fin n`. -/
def totalOrderDAG (n : ℕ) : Fin n → Fin n → Prop := fun i j => i < j

/-
Strict total-order dependency networks are acyclic.
-/
theorem totalOrderDAG_acyclic (n : ℕ) : Acyclic (totalOrderDAG n) := by
  intro v h;
  have h_trans : ∀ i j : Fin n, Relation.TransGen (fun i j : Fin n => i < j) i j → i < j := by
    intro i j hij; induction hij <;> [ tauto; exact lt_trans ‹_› ‹_› ] ;
  exact lt_irrefl _ ( h_trans _ _ h )

/-
Deleting any vertex from a total-order dependency network leaves all surviving
vertices weakly connected.  This gives an infinite family of acyclic networks with no
single-vertex weak-connectivity fragility.
-/
theorem totalOrderDAG_robust_after_deletion (n : ℕ) (deleted a b : Fin n)
    (ha : a ≠ deleted) (hb : b ≠ deleted) :
    AvoidingWalk (totalOrderDAG n) deleted a b := by
  rcases eq_or_ne a b with rfl | hab;
  · exact AvoidingWalk.refl ha;
  · cases lt_or_gt_of_ne hab <;> [ exact AvoidingWalk.step ha ( Or.inl ( by tauto ) ) ( AvoidingWalk.refl hb ) ; exact AvoidingWalk.step ha ( Or.inr ( by tauto ) ) ( AvoidingWalk.refl hb ) ]

/-
In particular, for every size at least three there is a nontrivial acyclic network,
with three distinct named vertices, whose deletion at an arbitrary vertex preserves weak
connectivity among all survivors.
-/
theorem exists_robust_acyclic_family (n : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n) :
    ∃ R : Fin n → Fin n → Prop,
      Acyclic R ∧
      (∃ x y z : Fin n, x ≠ y ∧ x ≠ z ∧ y ≠ z) ∧
      ∀ deleted a b, a ≠ deleted → b ≠ deleted → AvoidingWalk R deleted a b := by
  use totalOrderDAG n;
  exact ⟨ totalOrderDAG_acyclic n, by
    exact ⟨ ⟨ 0, by linarith ⟩, ⟨ 1, by linarith ⟩, ⟨ 2, by linarith ⟩, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num ⟩, totalOrderDAG_robust_after_deletion n ⟩

end ProofDAGStructure

The formal counterexample family uses the strict total order on `n` vertices: there is an edge `i → j` exactly when `i < j`. Direct enumeration gives:

The claim that acyclicity itself makes a dependency network fragile fails throughout the tested family. Every tested order network is acyclic, yet no vertex deletion weakly disconnects its survivors. The proof establishes this for every finite `n`, not merely the table above.

The edge-count sequence `0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, …` is the triangular-number sequence, OEIS A000217. No external sequence identification is needed for the structural proofs.

No corpus-wide Mathlib dependency graph was extracted in this cycle, so the proposed numerical exponent and historical top-ten ranking remain untested empirical hypotheses.
